extracted.intended_audience: prospective newspaper reporters and editors (sports and society departments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and editing newspaper sports copy (advance, review, and general game stories) and society-page items (engagements, weddings, teas, clubs, charity benefits, personals, seasonal reviews), emphasizing information-gathering, tone, and typographical/style conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 248. Obtaining Information
rubrics_metrics.description: In reporting games and contests one will have little difficulty in obtaining all needed information. Tickets are provided gratis and admit always to the best seats, known as the press seats, or the press-box, where all the newspaper men are grouped together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the contest is an outdoor meet, the press-box is usually on the top of the bleachers. Here are installed telegraph and telephone wires, the papers often having private wires from their offices to the field. If the wires have not been installed and it is necessary to report between quarters or halves, or inning by inning, one should have the local telegraph company provide at least two messengers to take the bulletins as fast as one writes them. And one's notes should be so taken that the bulletins may be given the messengers within a few seconds after it is possible to report.

rubrics_metrics.name: 249. Personal Opinion in Sporting Stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Three of the four kinds of sporting news — those dealing with athletic events before their occurrence, those dealing with the same events afterward, and those relating to sports in general — vary somewhat from the normal type of newspaper story, being hybrids partaking of the nature of both the pure news story and the editorial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The variance lies in the fact that these types may be either presenters or interpreters of sporting news, or both. The purpose of the news story is to present news; of the editorial, to interpret. Thus such sporting pieces may include personal opinion or advocacy (as in the example 'Michigan has a chance'), making a story half editorial and half news. Be aware of the dual role and craft the piece accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: 260. Advance Stories (what to include)
rubrics_metrics.description: The details which one may include in advance stories of athletic meets are innumerable. Some of the more important particulars, however, are predictions of the outcome, the effect of the contest on future events or on the rank of the teams, names of the players and the officials, absence of important men, opinions of the men, their trainers, or their followers, weak spots in their play, local or national interest, time and place of the contest, ways of reaching the field or grounds, — in fact, any details that will interest one's readers in the approaching game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such preliminary writeups require good reporters — men who can observe closely and analyze carefully, and hence can give their readers reasonable predictions of the success of the teams in which they are interested. Include practical logistics (routes, directions for finding seats) and human-interest context (prominent officials, crowd color) as illustrated by the 'Prominent Officials at Game To-day' example.

rubrics_metrics.name: 261. Review Stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories written days after a game are generally of an analytical nature, their purpose being to review the play or contest and explain why one team or contestant was successful and the other a failure, or why one method of play, attack, or defense proved better than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes such stories are merely individual incidents learned late, but of interest nevertheless. Use analysis to explain causes (e.g., rule changes, strategic differences) and to place the contest in historical or tactical context, as in the example 'New Rules Upset Teams.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 262. General Stories (Sports)
rubrics_metrics.description: The type of sporting news relating to a sport only in a general way may be considered briefly. In this type the actual news value is small; the interest of the story lies rather in its informative worth, the writer's purpose being to present general but significant facts that will interest followers of the sport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually expository; valuable for Sunday editions and as feature stories when athletic news is scarce. Typical subjects include comparative analyses (e.g., 'Batters in the American Association Weaker in 1916 than in 1915'), historical perspectives, popularity trends, and profiles ('Ty Cobb's Place in Baseball History').

rubrics_metrics.name: 263. What Society News Is
rubrics_metrics.description: The society editor's work concerns itself with the social and personal news of the city and county in which the paper is published or from which it draws its patronage. It is almost entirely local, news of the state or of other cities being of value only in so far as it affects women and men of one's own town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The society page does not concern itself with the unconventional or abnormal; elopements, clandestine marriages, unusual engagements, freakish parties, and similar extraordinary social and personal news do not come within the sphere of the society editor but take regular and usually prominent places in the news columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: 264. Difficulty (tone, discrimination, restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: The society editor's work is with the conventional in the local fashionable world, and for this reason probably no other kind of news demands so consistent care, discrimination, and habitual restraint. She must recognize readily relative social distinctions, to know what names and functions to feature in her column or section, and to be able to present the details of those functions acceptably to the various social groups about which and for which she is writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care not to overstep the narrow limits of conventional usage and make oneself ridiculous by extravagance of statement; avoid trite, colorless words and stock phrases. Maintain restraint and dignity of tone in write-ups of weddings, dances, receptions, and similar items.

rubrics_metrics.name: 266. Illustrations (accepted methods of handling society write-ups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected stories of engagements, weddings, dinners, dances, receptions, club meetings, and charity benefits are given to show the accepted methods of handling society write-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the restraint and dignity of tone in the examples. Use the provided formats (engagements, weddings, teas, receptions, personals) as models for structure and level of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagements (how to announce engagements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical engagement notices give the names of the announcing parents, the engaged couple, and brief background on the parties involved (family residence, education, affiliations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep announcements concise and factual: include full names, parents' names and addresses, and short relevant biographical notes (education, club memberships, profession) and note the expected timing of the wedding where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedding Announcements (content and tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wedding announcements should give the place and time of the ceremony, officiant, attendants, who gave the bride away, descriptions of gowns and veils, flowers, reception details, and the couple's immediate plans (tour, residence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide social context (notable guests, sponsors), present decorative details succinctly (gown materials, bouquet components), and preserve a restrained, dignified tone rather than extravagant phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teas, Dinners, Luncheons (reporting social events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of teas, dinners, and luncheons include host and hostess, assistants or who presided, decorations, attire of principal persons, origin or notable background of guests, and special features of the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey atmosphere through selective details (drawing room and dining room transformed into bowers of blossoms; music; favors) while keeping the account readable and not overly florid. Mention who presided and any notable social or official connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dances and Balls (reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of balls and themed dances should note the theme, costumes, drapery and decorations, menu or dinner features if given, number of guests, and notable costuming or social highlights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evocative but controlled description (e.g., 'bejeweled turbans; Chinese mandarins in long flowing coats') and list prominent attendees where relevant. Emphasize color and spectacle in moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Club Meeting Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Club meeting reports should name the club, note the program or speaker, summarize the remarks or subject (e.g., 'The Work of Women in Journalism'), and record any actions of the executive board or committee appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include prominent quotations, the speaker's main points, and any practical outcomes (voting, cooperation with other organizations). Provide the date/place and names of officers where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity Benefit Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity-benefit notices should state the beneficiary (e.g., 'Appui aux Artistes of France'), program features (talks, illustrated slides, musical performances), ticket price and contact for tickets, and the executive committee in charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention notable speakers or performers, the purpose of the benefit, admission price, and organizing committee names to confer legitimacy and encourage attendance or donations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personals (community updates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personals include short community notes: returns from trips, changes of residence, convalescences, births, and other brief personal news of local families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep items concise, factual, and locally relevant; include addresses and brief context (reason for travel, duration, names of family members) as in the examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society in Prospect and Review (seasonal overviews and features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seasonal prospect-and-review pieces survey the social season: upcoming events, schedules (dances, subscription dances), notable dinners and receptions, debutante activity, and social patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a narrative overview that captures the tempo and highlights of the season (who entertained, which families are prominent, dancing schedules). Use this form to give readers a sense of social calendar intensity and notable social movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 266. Clubs (covering women's clubs and constructive news)
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular attention of the prospective society editor may be called to club news. The work in literature, education, community betterment, general social relief, and kindred subjects now being undertaken by women's clubs is sometimes phenomenal and offers ... a vast undeveloped field for constructive news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid filling the page with dull routine copy; feature new studies and constructive efforts (campaigns against flies, garbage questions, comforts for slum children) with attractive individual heads to interest a large percentage of intelligent women in the community.
